name: GPSTR / CST 2026 — Days 1–2 questions (26–27 Sep)
description: Higher-difficulty questions for the study-plan topics of 26–27 September: Paper 2 Unit 1 and C/programming basics, plus Paper 1 psychology, GK, Kannada, computer literacy, English, health and value education.

questions.question: Which unit of the CPU generates the timing and control signals that direct the sequence of micro-operations, but does not itself operate on data?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: The control unit decodes instructions and issues control signals; the ALU performs the actual arithmetic and logic operations.

questions.question: The 'von Neumann bottleneck' refers to:

options.A: The limited width of the ALU
options.B: The absence of cache memory in early computers
options.C: The slow speed of secondary storage compared with RAM
options.D: The single shared pathway between CPU and memory used for both instructions and data

questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: In the von Neumann design, instructions and data travel over the same bus, so the CPU often waits for memory transfers.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The Harvard architecture uses separate memories/buses for instructions and data.
II. Most modern CPUs follow a modified Harvard design with split L1 instruction and data caches.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: Both are correct: pure Harvard separates instruction and data memory; modern CPUs split only the L1 caches while sharing main memory (modified Harvard).

questions.question: Which register holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: The PC always points to the next instruction; its value is copied to the MAR at the start of the fetch cycle.

questions.question: Which sequence of register transfers correctly describes the instruction fetch cycle?

options.A: IR ← PC; MAR ← IR; MBR ← M[MAR]
options.B: MBR ← PC; IR ← MBR; MAR ← IR
options.C: MAR ← PC; MBR ← M[MAR], PC ← PC + 1; IR ← MBR
options.D: PC ← MAR; IR ← M[PC]; MBR ← IR

questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: The PC is copied to the MAR, memory is read into the MBR while the PC is incremented, and the instruction moves from the MBR to the IR.

questions.question: The 'stored-program concept' introduced by John von Neumann means that:

options.A: Instructions and data reside in the same read–write memory, so a program can be loaded and modified like data
options.B: Programs are permanently stored in ROM
options.C: Programs are stored only on magnetic disks
options.D: Programs are hard-wired into the control unit

questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: Before the stored-program idea, machines like ENIAC were programmed by rewiring; storing instructions in memory made computers general-purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five classic functional units of a computer?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: The five units are input, output, memory, ALU and control unit. A compiler is software, not a functional hardware unit.

questions.question: A processor has a 32-bit address bus and byte-addressable memory. What is the maximum memory it can address directly?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: 2^32 addresses × 1 byte = 4,294,967,296 bytes = 4 GB.

questions.question: After adding two signed (two's complement) numbers, which status flag indicates that the result is outside the representable range?
questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: The overflow flag signals signed overflow; the carry flag signals an unsigned carry out of the most significant bit.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Widening the data bus can improve performance even at the same clock frequency.
Reason (R): A wider data bus transfers more bits in each bus cycle.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Introduction & Functional Components
questions.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: more bits per transfer means fewer bus cycles for the same amount of data.

questions.question: Which generation–technology pairing is INCORRECT?

options.C: Fifth generation – ULSI, parallel processing and AI

questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: Third generation computers used integrated circuits; microprocessors (VLSI) characterise the fourth generation.

questions.question: ENIAC, completed in 1945–46, used approximately how many vacuum tubes?
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: ENIAC had roughly 17,468 vacuum tubes, weighed about 27 tonnes and consumed around 150 kW of power.

questions.question: The Intel 4004 (1971), the first commercial single-chip microprocessor, was a:
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: The 4004 was a 4-bit CPU designed for a calculator; the 8008 (1972) and 8080 (1974) were 8-bit.

questions.question: In Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, the 'Mill' corresponds to which part of a modern computer?
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: The 'Store' held numbers (memory) and the 'Mill' performed calculations (processor/ALU); punched cards gave input.

questions.question: Which machine is credited with running the world's first stored program, in June 1948?
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: The Small-Scale Experimental Machine at Manchester ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948; EDSAC (1949) was the first practical one.

questions.question: A computer in a hospital ICU accepts continuous signals such as heartbeat and temperature, converts them to digital form and processes them. It is an example of a:
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: Hybrid computers combine analog input handling with digital processing, as in ICU patient monitors.

questions.question: India's first supercomputer, PARAM 8000 (1991), was developed by:
questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: The Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) built PARAM 8000 after India was denied import of a Cray supercomputer.

questions.question: UNIVAC I (1951) is notable because it was:

options.A: The first commercially produced computer in the United States
options.C: The first computer to use integrated circuits

questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: UNIVAC I was the first commercial computer produced in the US; it famously predicted the 1952 presidential election.

questions.question: Moore's law, in its commonly cited (1975) form, states that:

options.A: Memory prices halve every six months
options.B: Processor power consumption doubles every five years
options.D: The number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles about every two years

questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: Gordon Moore observed that transistor count doubles roughly every two years; clock speed is not part of the law.

questions.question: Arrange in chronological order: Pascaline, Jacquard loom, Abacus, Analytical Engine.

options.A: Abacus → Pascaline → Jacquard loom → Analytical Engine
options.B: Abacus → Jacquard loom → Pascaline → Analytical Engine
options.C: Pascaline → Abacus → Jacquard loom → Analytical Engine
options.D: Abacus → Pascaline → Analytical Engine → Jacquard loom

questions.subject: Evolution, Generations, Classification, Applications
questions.explanation: Abacus (ancient), Pascaline (1642), Jacquard's punched-card loom (1804) and Babbage's Analytical Engine design (1837).

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-impact printer?
questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: Laser and inkjet printers form images without striking the paper; dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line printers are impact printers.

questions.question: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) is mainly used for:

options.B: Converting scanned text to editable text

questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: Cheques carry the MICR line printed in magnetic ink (E-13B font), which machines read quickly and reliably.

questions.question: The print quality (resolution) of a laser printer is usually expressed in:
questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: DPI (dots per inch) measures resolution; PPM (pages per minute) measures speed.

questions.question: Which of the following memories is volatile?
questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: SRAM (like DRAM) loses its contents when power is removed; ROM, EEPROM and flash are non-volatile.

questions.question: DRAM must be refreshed periodically because:

options.B: It stores bits in flip-flops that lose state
options.C: Each bit is stored as charge on a capacitor that gradually leaks

questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: A DRAM cell is a transistor and a capacitor; the charge leaks within milliseconds, so it is refreshed. SRAM uses flip-flops and needs no refresh.

questions.question: Arrange in order of decreasing access speed:

options.A: Registers > Cache > Main memory > SSD > Hard disk
options.B: Cache > Registers > Main memory > Hard disk > SSD
options.C: Registers > Main memory > Cache > SSD > Hard disk
options.D: Cache > Main memory > Registers > SSD > Hard disk

questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: Registers are fastest, then cache (SRAM), main memory (DRAM), SSD (flash) and finally the mechanical hard disk.

questions.question: The contents of an EPROM chip are erased by:
questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: EPROM has a quartz window for UV erasure; EEPROM and flash are erased electrically.

questions.question: Most smartphone touch screens detect a finger through a change in the electrostatic field. They are:
questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: Capacitive screens sense the conductive human body; resistive screens respond to pressure and work with any stylus.

questions.question: Plotters are preferred over ordinary printers mainly for:

options.A: Large-format vector drawings such as engineering and CAD drawings

questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: Plotters draw continuous lines with pens or inkjets on large sheets, which suits maps and CAD drawings.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched?

options.C: OCR – reads characters printed in magnetic ink
options.D: OMR – detects marks made in predefined positions

questions.subject: Input, Output and Memory Devices
questions.explanation: OMR reads pencil/pen marks (e.g. answer sheets); OCR recognises printed text; MICR reads magnetic ink; BCR reads barcodes.

questions.question: According to Donald Knuth, which of the following is NOT an essential property of an algorithm?

options.A: It must take at least one input

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: An algorithm has zero or more inputs and one or more outputs, and must be finite, definite and effective.

questions.question: Which of the following is system software?
questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Device drivers let the OS control hardware; they are system software. The others are application software.

questions.question: Firmware is best described as:

options.C: Software permanently stored in ROM/flash that controls a hardware device
options.D: Software whose source code is public

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: BIOS/UEFI and the code inside routers or printers are firmware, stored in non-volatile memory on the device.

questions.question: Pseudocode is:

options.B: Code that the compiler translates directly
options.D: An informal, language-independent description of an algorithm's logic

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Pseudocode uses structured English-like statements to plan logic before coding in any particular language.

questions.question: Which kind of licence allows users to run, study, modify and redistribute the source code?

options.D: Free and open-source licence (e.g. GNU GPL)

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Freeware is free of cost but usually closed; open-source licences like the GPL grant the freedom to modify and share the code.

questions.question: The 'top-down' approach to problem solving means:

options.B: Writing the detailed code first and combining it later
options.C: Breaking the main problem into smaller sub-problems by stepwise refinement
options.D: Testing the program before designing it

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Top-down design starts from the overall problem and refines it into modules; bottom-up design builds from small components.

questions.question:
What is printed by this algorithm?
sum ← 0
for i ← 1 to 5
  if i mod 2 = 1 then sum ← sum + i
print sum
questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Only odd values of i are added: 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

questions.question: Which of the following is a utility program?
questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Utilities (defragmenters, antivirus, backup tools) help maintain the computer; the others are application software.

questions.question: A trace table is used to:

options.A: Dry-run an algorithm by recording the values of variables at each step

questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: Dry-running with a trace table helps find logical errors before the program is executed.

questions.question: In a flowchart, which symbol is used for a connector joining different parts of the chart?
questions.subject: Software Concepts & Problem Solving Methodology
questions.explanation: A small circle is an on-page connector; rectangle = process, diamond = decision, parallelogram = input/output.

questions.question: In MS Excel, how many cells are added by =SUM(A1:B3)?
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: A1:B3 is 2 columns × 3 rows = 6 cells.

questions.question: In the Excel reference $A1:

options.A: The column is absolute and the row is relative
options.B: The row is absolute and the column is relative
options.C: Both row and column are absolute
options.D: Both row and column are relative

questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: The $ fixes the part it precedes: $A1 keeps column A fixed while the row changes when copied.

questions.question: Cell C1 contains =A1*$B$1. If it is copied to C3, the formula in C3 becomes:
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: The relative reference A1 shifts by two rows to A3; the absolute reference $B$1 does not change.

questions.question: Mail Merge in MS Word combines:

options.A: A main document with a data source to produce personalised copies

questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: Mail Merge fills fields (name, address…) from a data source such as an Excel sheet into a letter template.

questions.question: Which PowerPoint view lets you rearrange slides by dragging their thumbnails, all on one screen?
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: Slide Sorter shows all slides as thumbnails for reordering, deleting and applying transitions.

questions.question: Cells A1:A5 contain 10, "abc", (blank), 5 and TRUE. What does =COUNT(A1:A5) return?
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: COUNT counts only numeric values. Text, blanks and logical values inside a range are ignored, so only 10 and 5 are counted. COUNTA would return 4.

questions.question: Which Excel error appears when a formula refers to a cell that is no longer valid, for example because it was deleted?
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: #REF! means an invalid reference; #NAME? an unknown function name; #VALUE! a wrong type of argument; #N/A a value not available.

questions.question: In MS Word, the shortcut Ctrl+J is used to:
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: Ctrl+J justifies, Ctrl+E centres, Ctrl+K inserts a hyperlink and Ctrl+G opens Go To.

questions.question: In PowerPoint, changes made to the Slide Master:

options.A: Apply the theme, layouts and fonts to all slides based on it

questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: The Slide Master stores the design shared by all slides, so one change updates the whole presentation.

questions.question: A1 = 60 and B1 = 50. What does =IF(AND(A1>50, B1>50), "Pass", "Fail") return?
questions.subject: Word Processing, Spreadsheets, PowerPoint
questions.explanation: B1>50 is FALSE because 50 is not greater than 50, so AND returns FALSE and the formula gives "Fail".

questions.question: In traditional chipsets, which component linked the CPU with RAM and the graphics slot (the high-speed devices)?
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: The northbridge handled high-speed links (memory, AGP/PCIe graphics); the southbridge handled slower I/O such as USB, SATA and audio.

questions.question: The CMOS battery on a motherboard is used to:

options.A: Power the CPU when the mains supply fails
options.B: Keep the real-time clock running and retain BIOS settings when the PC is off
options.D: Supply power to the hard disk

questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: A coin cell (CR2032) keeps the RTC and the CMOS settings alive while the computer is unplugged.

questions.question: The Power-On Self-Test (POST) is performed by:
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: POST runs from firmware immediately after power-on, before any operating system is loaded.

questions.question: Which of these motherboard form factors is the smallest?
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: Mini-ITX is 17 × 17 cm; Micro-ATX is 24.4 × 24.4 cm; ATX is 30.5 × 24.4 cm; E-ATX is larger still.

questions.question: On modern motherboards, the M.2 slot is mainly used for:

options.C: NVMe/SATA solid-state drives (and some Wi-Fi cards)

questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: M.2 is a small edge connector used mostly for NVMe SSDs running over PCIe lanes.

questions.question: In modern Intel and AMD platforms, the memory controller that used to be in the northbridge is now located in:
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: Integrating the memory controller into the CPU reduces memory latency; the remaining I/O functions sit in the PCH/chipset.

questions.question: Modern graphics cards are installed in which type of expansion slot?
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: PCIe x16 provides the bandwidth that graphics cards need; AGP and ISA are obsolete.

questions.question: SO-DIMM memory modules are mainly used in:
questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: SO-DIMMs are about half the length of desktop DIMMs, which suits laptops and mini PCs.

questions.question: Which feature is provided by UEFI but not by legacy BIOS?

options.A: Secure Boot and booting from GPT disks larger than 2 TB

questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: UEFI supports GPT partitioning, Secure Boot and faster booting; POST, boot order and CMOS settings existed in legacy BIOS too.

questions.question: DDR SDRAM achieves higher bandwidth than SDR SDRAM at the same clock because it:

options.A: Transfers data on both the rising and falling edges of the clock
options.D: Doubles the storage capacity of each chip

questions.subject: Computer Configuration & Motherboard
questions.explanation: Double Data Rate means two transfers per clock cycle.

questions.question: An SMPS in a computer converts:

options.A: AC mains supply into regulated low-voltage DC (12 V, 5 V, 3.3 V)
options.B: Battery DC into AC for the monitor

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: The switched-mode power supply rectifies and regulates the mains supply into the DC rails needed by the components.

questions.question: How many pins does the main ATX power connector on a modern motherboard have?
questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: The main ATX connector has 24 pins (older boards used 20); the separate 4/8-pin EPS connector powers the CPU.

questions.question: Thermal paste is applied between the CPU and its heat sink to:

options.B: Fill microscopic air gaps and improve heat transfer

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: Air is a poor conductor; a thin layer of thermal paste fills surface irregularities so heat flows to the heat sink.

questions.question: Which UPS type provides virtually zero switch-over time because the load always runs from the inverter?
questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: An online UPS continuously converts AC→DC→AC, so there is no transfer delay when mains power fails.

questions.question: Cache memory is usually built from:
questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: SRAM is faster than DRAM and needs no refresh, which suits small, fast cache memory.

questions.question: Virtual memory allows a computer to:

options.C: Use cache as a hard disk
options.D: Use part of secondary storage as an extension of main memory

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: Pages are swapped between RAM and a page file or swap space on disk, so programs can be larger than physical RAM.

questions.question: How many bytes are there in 2 MiB?
questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling

questions.question: An '80 PLUS' certification on a PC power supply indicates:

options.A: At least 80% energy efficiency at 20%, 50% and 100% load

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: 80 PLUS certifies efficiency; higher grades (Bronze, Silver, Gold…) require even better efficiency.

questions.question: Which is recommended practice when assembling a desktop computer?

options.A: Install the CPU, cooler and RAM on the motherboard before fixing it in the cabinet
options.B: Apply thermal paste after fixing the heat sink
options.C: Connect the power cord before installing the RAM
options.D: Keep the PSU switched on while installing components

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: Components are easier and safer to fit on an open board; all work is done with the power disconnected.

questions.question: An anti-static wrist strap is worn while assembling a computer to:

options.B: Protect against electric shock from the mains
options.D: Prevent electrostatic discharge damage to components

questions.subject: Memory, Power Supply & Assembling
questions.explanation: Static charge from the body can destroy sensitive chips; the strap keeps you at the same potential as the chassis.

questions.question: Which language–paradigm pair is INCORRECT?
questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: Haskell is a purely functional language; Prolog is the classic logic-programming language.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the main phases of a compiler?

options.A: Lexical analysis → Syntax analysis → Semantic analysis → Intermediate code → Optimisation → Code generation
options.B: Syntax analysis → Lexical analysis → Semantic analysis → Code generation → Optimisation
options.C: Lexical analysis → Semantic analysis → Syntax analysis → Optimisation → Code generation
options.D: Parsing → Scanning → Code generation → Semantic analysis

questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: The scanner produces tokens, the parser builds a parse tree, semantic analysis checks types, then IR is generated, optimised and translated to target code.

questions.question: The output of the lexical analyser is a stream of:
questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: The lexical analyser (scanner) groups characters into tokens such as identifiers, keywords and operators.

questions.question: Which formal model is used to recognise the context-free syntax of programming languages?
questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: Context-free grammars are recognised by pushdown automata; finite automata recognise the regular languages used in lexical analysis.

questions.question: A grammar is said to be ambiguous if:

options.B: Some string has more than one parse tree (or leftmost derivation)

questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: Ambiguity means one sentence can be derived in two different ways, e.g. the classic dangling-else problem.

questions.question: In a dynamically typed language such as Python, the type of a variable is bound:
questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: Dynamic typing binds types to values during execution; C and Java bind types at compile time.

questions.question: Which statement is generally TRUE?

options.A: A compiler cannot detect syntax errors
options.B: An interpreter translates the whole program before running any part
options.C: An interpreter produces a standalone object file
options.D: Compiled programs usually run faster than the same program interpreted

questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: A compiler translates the whole program in advance into machine code; an interpreter translates and executes statement by statement, which is slower.

questions.question: 'Orthogonality' in programming language design means:

options.A: Every statement must end with a semicolon
options.B: The language has no data types
options.C: The language supports only right-angled graphics
options.D: A small set of primitive constructs can be combined in few ways, and every combination is legal and meaningful

questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: High orthogonality reduces exceptions to the rules, making a language easier to learn and read.

questions.question: Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation, as used by the Java Virtual Machine, means:

options.A: Compilation happens on a remote server
options.B: Source code is compiled only once, at installation
options.C: Bytecode is compiled into native machine code at run time, when needed

questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: The JVM interprets bytecode and compiles frequently used parts (hot spots) into native code while the program runs.

questions.question: BNF (Backus–Naur Form) is used to describe the:
questions.subject: Language Design and Translation Issues
questions.explanation: BNF/EBNF notations formally specify the context-free syntax of programming languages.

questions.question: Which of the following is a composite (structured) data type?
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Arrays, structures and records are composite; int, char, float and enum are scalar (elementary) types.

questions.question: A language is called 'strongly typed' if:

options.B: All type errors are always detected (at compile or run time)
options.C: Variables must be declared in upper case

questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Strong typing guarantees that type errors are caught; C is weakly typed because of unchecked casts and unions.

questions.question: In C, the value of sizeof(char) is:
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: The C standard defines sizeof(char) as exactly 1 (one byte), whatever the number of bits in a byte.

questions.question: What is the range of an 8-bit signed integer stored in two's complement?
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: An n-bit two's complement number ranges from −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1, i.e. −128 to +127 for 8 bits.

questions.question: The automatic conversion of an int to a float in the expression 5 + 2.5 is called:
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Coercion is done by the compiler implicitly; casting is written explicitly by the programmer, e.g. (float)5.

questions.question: Two types are considered the same under 'structural equivalence' if:

options.A: They occupy the same memory address
options.B: They are declared in the same statement
options.C: They have identical structure (same components in the same order)

questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Name equivalence requires the same type name; structural equivalence compares the type structure.

questions.question: In the IEEE 754 single-precision format, the numbers of sign, exponent and fraction bits are:
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Single precision (32 bits) = 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 fraction bits; double precision = 1 + 11 + 52.

questions.question: In C, given enum colour { RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE };  what is the value of BLUE?
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: RED = 0, GREEN is explicitly 5, and each following enumerator is one more than the previous one, so BLUE = 6.

questions.question: A descriptor (such as a dope vector for arrays) stores:

options.A: The attributes of a data object, such as its type, bounds and address
options.B: Only the value of the variable
options.C: The source code of a function

questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: Descriptors hold the information needed to access a data object, e.g. array bounds for index checking.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a scalar (elementary) type in C?
questions.subject: Elementary Data Types
questions.explanation: A struct groups several members, so it is a composite type.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: Integer division truncates 10/3 to 3, and 10 % 3 = 1.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: The array includes the terminating '\0', so sizeof is 6; strlen counts only the 5 visible characters.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: Execution starts at case 2 and falls through to case 3 because there is no break after case 2; the break then stops before default.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: The semicolon after the for makes an empty loop body; the loop ends when i becomes 5, then printf runs once.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid C identifier?
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: Identifiers may start with a letter or underscore and cannot be keywords or contain '-'.

questions.question:
Assuming a 4-byte int, what is sizeof(u) for:
union { int i; char c[8]; } u;
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: A union is as large as its largest member (8 bytes here); a struct would need space for all members.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: When an array is partly initialised, the remaining elements are set to zero.

questions.question:
What is the value of x?
int x = 2 + 3 * 4 > 10 && 5;
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: A do-while body executes at least once before the condition is checked.

questions.question: On a typical system with 4-byte int and 4-byte alignment, sizeof(struct { char c; int i; }) is:
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 1
questions.explanation: Three padding bytes are inserted after c so that i starts on a 4-byte boundary: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: p + 2 points to a[2], and dereferencing it gives 30.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: **q is the same object as *p, which is x, so x becomes 10.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: C passes arguments by value; f changes only its local copy n.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: A static local variable is initialised once and keeps its value between calls: 1, 2, 3.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: The macro expands to 2+3*2+3 = 2 + 6 + 3 = 11. Writing ((x)*(x)) would give 25.

questions.question:
A program is run as:  ./prog one two
What is the value of argc?
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: argv[0] is the program name, so argc counts it too: prog, one, two = 3.

questions.question: Which statement about fopen("data.txt", "a") is correct?

options.A: It fails if the file does not exist
options.B: It opens the file for appending and creates it if it does not exist
options.C: It truncates the file to zero length
options.D: It opens the file for reading only

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: Mode "a" writes at the end of the file and creates the file if needed; "w" truncates; "r" fails if the file is missing.

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: s + 1 points to the second character, 'B'.

questions.question: A pointer p of type int* holds address 1000, and sizeof(int) is 4. After p++, p holds:
questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the pointed-to type: 1000 + 1 × 4 = 1004.

questions.question: Which statement is true of calloc() but not of malloc()?

options.C: It initialises the allocated memory to zero
options.D: It allocates memory on the heap

questions.subject: Programming in C – Part 2
questions.explanation: Both allocate heap memory, return void* and can return NULL; only calloc zero-fills the block.

questions.question: Over time, psychology was successively defined as the science of:
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: The meaning shifted from the Greek 'psyche' (soul) to mind, then consciousness (Wundt, James) and finally behaviour (Watson).

questions.question: Who defined psychology as 'the science of behaviour'?
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Watson, founder of behaviourism (1913), rejected the study of consciousness in favour of observable behaviour.

questions.question: 'First psychology lost its soul, then it lost its mind, then it lost consciousness; it still has behaviour of a sort.' This remark is attributed to:
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Woodworth used this remark to summarise how the definition of psychology changed.

questions.question: The first psychological laboratory was established in 1879 by:
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Wundt's Leipzig laboratory marks the start of experimental psychology as a separate science.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the father of educational psychology?
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Thorndike's work 'Educational Psychology' (1903) and his laws of learning founded the field.

questions.question: 'Educational psychology is that branch of psychology which deals with teaching and learning.' This definition was given by:
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: The definition is by Charles E. Skinner, the educational psychologist, not the behaviourist B. F. Skinner.

questions.question: The nature of educational psychology is best described as:

options.B: A normative science that prescribes ideals
options.D: An applied, positive science of behaviour in educational situations

questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: It applies psychological principles to education and describes 'what is' rather than prescribing 'what ought to be'.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually included in the scope of educational psychology?
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Its scope covers the learner, learning process, learning situation, evaluation and the teacher, not administrative pay matters.

questions.question: Which school–founder pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Gestalt psychology was founded by Max Wertheimer, with Köhler and Koffka; Watson founded behaviourism.

questions.question: The principle 'the whole is different from (greater than) the sum of its parts' is central to:
questions.subject: Psychology & Educational Psychology
questions.explanation: Gestalt psychologists stressed perceiving organised wholes, which led to insight learning (Köhler).

questions.question: Which method of psychology is least suitable for studying young children and people with mental disorders?
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: Introspection needs a trained, articulate person to examine their own mental states, which young children cannot do.

questions.question: The introspection method was mainly developed by the:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: Structuralists trained observers to report the elements of their conscious experience.

questions.question: In an experiment on the effect of praise on pupils' test scores, 'praise' is the:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: The experimenter manipulates the independent variable (praise) and measures the dependent variable (test scores).

questions.question: A teacher studies a chronically absent pupil in depth, collecting family history, health records and interviews. This is the:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: A case study is an intensive, many-sided study of one individual, often a problem child.

questions.question: When the observer joins the group and takes part in its activities while observing, it is called:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: In participant observation the observer becomes a member of the group being studied.

questions.question: The main purpose of a control group in an experiment is to:

options.B: Replace the experimental group if it fails
options.D: Provide a baseline for comparison with the experimental group

questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: The control group does not receive the treatment, so any difference can be attributed to the independent variable.

questions.question: People change their behaviour simply because they know they are being studied. This limitation of observation is known as the:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: The name comes from the Hawthorne Works studies (1920s–30s), where workers' productivity rose because they were being observed.

questions.question: The experimental method is considered the most scientific method of psychology because it:

options.A: Establishes cause-and-effect relationships under controlled conditions
options.C: Studies only one person at a time

questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: Controlling other variables lets the researcher conclude that changes in the dependent variable were caused by the independent variable.

questions.question: Studying the same group of children from age 5 to 15 to track their development is the:
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: Longitudinal studies follow the same subjects over a long time; cross-sectional studies compare different age groups at one time.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Introspection is an objective method.
II. The experimental method can establish cause-and-effect relationships.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Methods of Psychology
questions.explanation: Introspection is subjective, since only the person can observe their own mind; statement II is correct.

questions.question: Which book did Jawaharlal Nehru write while imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort (1942–46)?

options.C: Letters from a Father to His Daughter

questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: The Discovery of India was written at Ahmednagar Fort; Glimpses of World History consists of letters written from prisons in 1930–33.

questions.question:
Match the books with their authors:
(a) Anandamath (b) Nil Darpan (c) Gita Govinda (d) Mudrarakshasa
1. Jayadeva 2. Dinabandhu Mitra 3. Vishakhadatta 4. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Anandamath (with 'Vande Mataram') is by Bankim Chandra, Nil Darpan by Dinabandhu Mitra, Gita Govinda by Jayadeva and Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta.

questions.question: The first Jnanpith Award for Kannada went to Kuvempu in 1967 for:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Kuvempu received the Jnanpith for his epic Sri Ramayana Darshanam; Malegalalli Madumagalu and Kanooru Heggadithi are his novels.

questions.question: K. Shivaram Karanth received the Jnanpith Award (1977) for:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Mookajjiya Kanasugalu won the Jnanpith; Chomana Dudi, Marali Mannige and Bettada Jeeva are his other well-known novels.

questions.question: Which book deeply influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who paraphrased it in Gujarati as 'Sarvodaya'?

options.C: The Kingdom of God Is Within You – Leo Tolstoy

questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Gandhi read Ruskin's Unto This Last in 1904 and translated its ideas as 'Sarvodaya' (welfare of all).

questions.question: 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India', which put forward the 'drain theory', was written by:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Dadabhai Naoroji argued that British rule drained India's wealth; R. C. Dutt wrote 'The Economic History of India'.

questions.question: The earliest available literary work in Kannada, a treatise on poetics (c. 850 CE), is:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Kavirajamarga, from the court of the Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I (attributed to Srivijaya), is the earliest extant Kannada work.

questions.question: Which pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Harshacharita, the biography of King Harsha, was written by Banabhatta.

questions.question: 'Wings of Fire', the autobiography of Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, was co-written with:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Wings of Fire (1999) was written with Arun Tiwari; Kalam wrote 'India 2020' with Y. S. Rajan.

questions.question: Adikavi Pampa's 'Vikramarjuna Vijaya' is popularly known as:
questions.subject: Famous Books and Authors
questions.explanation: Vikramarjuna Vijaya retells the Mahabharata (Pampa Bharata); Adipurana is Pampa's Jain work; Gadayuddha is by Ranna.

questions.question: Which discovery–scientist pair is INCORRECTLY matched?
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron (1897); Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus and the proton.

questions.question: National Science Day (28 February) commemorates the discovery of:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: C. V. Raman announced the Raman Effect on 28 February 1928 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1930.

questions.question: The first vaccine, against smallpox, was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796 using:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Jenner observed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not get smallpox, and inoculated people with cowpox material.

questions.question: The World Wide Web was invented in 1989 by Tim Berners-Lee at:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Berners-Lee proposed the WWW at CERN, Geneva, and wrote the first web browser and server.

questions.question: The transistor was invented in 1947 at Bell Labs by:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: The three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics; Kilby and Noyce invented the integrated circuit.

questions.question: Insulin was discovered in 1921 by:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Banting and Best isolated insulin at the University of Toronto; Banting shared the 1923 Nobel Prize with Macleod.

questions.question: The laws of electromagnetic induction were discovered by:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the basis of generators and transformers.

questions.question: The circulation of blood in the human body was described by:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Harvey published De Motu Cordis in 1628; Landsteiner discovered blood groups.

questions.question: Who proposed the heliocentric model, placing the Sun at the centre of the solar system?
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Copernicus published the heliocentric theory in 1543; Ptolemy's model was geocentric.

questions.question: Radioactivity was discovered in 1896 by:
questions.subject: Important Inventions and Discoveries
questions.explanation: Becquerel found that uranium salts emit radiation; the Curies later discovered polonium and radium. Röntgen discovered X-rays (1895).

questions.question: ಪ್ರಸ್ತುತ ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿರುವ ಒಟ್ಟು ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆ ಎಷ್ಟು?
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಸ್ವರಗಳು 13 + ಯೋಗವಾಹಗಳು 2 + ವ್ಯಂಜನಗಳು 34 = 49 ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳು.

questions.question: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿರುವ ಸ್ವರಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆ:
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಅ ಆ ಇ ಈ ಉ ಊ ಋ ಎ ಏ ಐ ಒ ಓ ಔ – ಒಟ್ಟು 13 ಸ್ವರಗಳು.

questions.question: ಯೋಗವಾಹಗಳು ಯಾವುವು?
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಅನುಸ್ವಾರ (ಂ) ಮತ್ತು ವಿಸರ್ಗ (ಃ) ಯೋಗವಾಹಗಳು; ಇವು ಸ್ವತಂತ್ರವಾಗಿ ಉಚ್ಚರಿಸಲ್ಪಡದೆ ಬೇರೆ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳ ಜೊತೆ ಸೇರಿ ಬರುತ್ತವೆ.

questions.question: ವರ್ಗೀಯ ಮತ್ತು ಅವರ್ಗೀಯ ವ್ಯಂಜನಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆ ಕ್ರಮವಾಗಿ:
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಕ, ಚ, ಟ, ತ, ಪ ಎಂಬ ಐದು ವರ್ಗಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ತಲಾ 5 = 25 ವರ್ಗೀಯ; ಯ ರ ಲ ವ ಶ ಷ ಸ ಹ ಳ = 9 ಅವರ್ಗೀಯ ವ್ಯಂಜನಗಳು.

questions.question: ಈ ಕೆಳಗಿನವುಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಅನುನಾಸಿಕ ಅಕ್ಷರ ಯಾವುದು?
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಪ್ರತಿ ವರ್ಗದ ಐದನೆಯ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳಾದ ಙ ಞ ಣ ನ ಮ ಅನುನಾಸಿಕಗಳು.

questions.question: ಕೆಳಗಿನವುಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಎಲ್ಲವೂ ಮಹಾಪ್ರಾಣ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳಾಗಿರುವ ಗುಂಪು:
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಪ್ರತಿ ವರ್ಗದ ಎರಡನೆಯ ಮತ್ತು ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳು (ಖ ಘ, ಛ ಝ, ಠ ಢ, ಥ ಧ, ಫ ಭ) ಮಹಾಪ್ರಾಣಗಳು – ಒಟ್ಟು 10.

questions.question: ಕೆಳಗಿನವುಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಎಲ್ಲವೂ ದೀರ್ಘ ಸ್ವರಗಳಾಗಿರುವ ಗುಂಪು:
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಹ್ರಸ್ವ ಸ್ವರಗಳು: ಅ ಇ ಉ ಋ ಎ ಒ (6). ದೀರ್ಘ ಸ್ವರಗಳು: ಆ ಈ ಊ ಏ ಐ ಓ ಔ (7).

questions.question: ಕೆಳಗಿನ ಪದಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಸಜಾತೀಯ ಸಂಯುಕ್ತಾಕ್ಷರವಿರುವ ಪದ ಯಾವುದು?
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಒಂದೇ ವ್ಯಂಜನ ಎರಡು ಬಾರಿ ಸೇರಿದರೆ ಸಜಾತೀಯ (ಮ್ + ಮ = ಮ್ಮ). ಶಕ್ತಿ (ಕ್+ತ), ವಿದ್ಯೆ (ದ್+ಯ), ಸ್ವರ (ಸ್+ವ) ವಿಜಾತೀಯ ಸಂಯುಕ್ತಾಕ್ಷರಗಳು.

questions.question: 'ಕಾ' ಎಂಬ ಗುಣಿತಾಕ್ಷರದಲ್ಲಿ ಸೇರಿರುವ ವರ್ಣಗಳು:
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಗುಣಿತಾಕ್ಷರ = ವ್ಯಂಜನ (ಅರ್ಧಾಕ್ಷರ) + ಸ್ವರ. ಕ್ + ಆ = ಕಾ.

questions.question: ಕೇಶಿರಾಜನು 'ಶಬ್ದಮಣಿದರ್ಪಣ'ದಲ್ಲಿ ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆಯ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳ ಸಂಖ್ಯೆಯನ್ನು ಎಷ್ಟೆಂದು ಹೇಳಿದ್ದಾನೆ?
questions.subject: ಕನ್ನಡ ವರ್ಣಮಾಲೆ
questions.explanation: ಕೇಶಿರಾಜನ ಪ್ರಕಾರ ಕನ್ನಡದ ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳು 47. ಪ್ರಸ್ತುತ ಶಾಲಾ ಪಠ್ಯಪುಸ್ತಕಗಳಲ್ಲಿ 49 ಅಕ್ಷರಗಳನ್ನು ಗುರುತಿಸಲಾಗಿದೆ.

questions.question: A computer inside an ATM or a washing-machine controller is an example of a:
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: Special-purpose computers are built for one dedicated task; general-purpose computers run many kinds of programs.

questions.question: SQL is classified as a:
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: 1GL = machine code, 2GL = assembly, 3GL = high-level languages like C, 4GL = non-procedural languages like SQL.

questions.question: Which program translates assembly language into machine code?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: An assembler converts mnemonics (MOV, ADD) into machine code; compilers and interpreters handle high-level languages.

questions.question: Which memory can the CPU access directly?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: Secondary storage must first be loaded into main memory before the CPU can use it.

questions.question: How many nibbles are there in 4 bytes?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: 1 byte = 8 bits = 2 nibbles, so 4 bytes = 8 nibbles.

questions.question: Which storage device uses flash memory and has no moving parts?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: SSDs store data in NAND flash chips, so they are faster and more shock-resistant than HDDs with spinning platters.

questions.question: A computer that supports hundreds of users at once for bulk transaction processing, such as railway reservations or banking, is typically a:
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: Mainframes (e.g. IBM Z) handle very large volumes of simultaneous transactions reliably.

questions.question: Which of these is hardware rather than software?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: A graphics card is a physical component; the BIOS is firmware, and drivers and compilers are software.

questions.question: Which language can be executed by the computer without any translation?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: Machine language (binary) is the only language the CPU understands directly.

questions.question: Which of these is a brand or type of operating system, not application software?
questions.subject: Unit 1 – Introduction to Computer
questions.explanation: Ubuntu is a Linux distribution (an operating system); the others are applications.

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: He ran FAST to catch the bus.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'Fast' modifies the verb 'ran', telling how he ran, so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: The FAST was broken after sunset.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: Here 'fast' means a period of not eating; it is the subject of the sentence, so it is a noun.

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: She is TOO tired to walk.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'Too' modifies the adjective 'tired', so it is an adverb (of degree).

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: BESIDES English, he speaks French.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'Besides' is followed by the noun 'English' as its object, so it is a preposition.

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: He came AFTER I had left.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'After' joins two clauses ('He came' and 'I had left'), so here it is a subordinating conjunction.

questions.question: Identify the part of speech of the word in capitals: ALAS! He is no more.
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'Alas' expresses sudden emotion (sorrow), so it is an interjection.

questions.question: In 'SWIMMING is good exercise', the word in capitals is:

options.A: A present participle used as an adjective

questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: An -ing form used as a noun (here the subject) is a gerund.

questions.question: In 'The RICH are not always happy', the word in capitals is used as a:
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'The rich' means rich people; an adjective preceded by 'the' can work as a plural noun.

questions.question: In 'This is the book THAT I bought yesterday', the word in capitals is a:
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'That' introduces a relative clause describing 'the book', so it is a relative pronoun.

questions.question: In 'She sings WELL', the word in capitals is a/an:
questions.subject: Parts of Speech
questions.explanation: 'Well' modifies the verb 'sings'. In 'She is well', it would be an adjective meaning healthy.

questions.question: Which dimension is NOT part of the WHO's original 1948 definition of health?
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: WHO (1948): 'Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.' The spiritual dimension was discussed later.

questions.question: World Health Day is observed every year on:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: It marks the founding of the WHO on 7 April 1948. 1 Dec is World AIDS Day, 31 May is World No Tobacco Day and 5 June is World Environment Day.

questions.question: The word 'hygiene' is derived from Hygieia, who in Greek mythology was the goddess of:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Hygieia, daughter of Asclepius, was the Greek goddess of health, cleanliness and sanitation.

questions.question: Screening school staff for diabetes to detect it early is an example of:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Secondary prevention means early diagnosis and prompt treatment; primary prevention (e.g. immunisation) stops disease from occurring.

questions.question: Immunisation of children is an example of:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Specific protection such as vaccination prevents the disease from occurring at all.

questions.question: The main aim of health education is to:

options.D: Bring desirable changes in people's health knowledge, attitudes and practices

questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Health education aims at voluntary behaviour change, often measured as KAP (knowledge, attitude, practice).

questions.question: Global Handwashing Day is observed on:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: 15 October promotes handwashing with soap; 2 October is Gandhi Jayanti and 22 March is World Water Day.

questions.question: Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: It was launched on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2014; India was declared open-defecation-free on 2 October 2019.

questions.question: According to the WHO, the normal Body Mass Index (BMI) range for adults is:
questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)². Below 18.5 is underweight, 25–29.9 overweight and 30 or more obese.

questions.question: Personal hygiene such as washing hands before eating mainly prevents diseases spread through the:

options.D: Faeco-oral route, e.g. typhoid and cholera

questions.subject: Health Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Contaminated hands carry germs from faeces to the mouth; handwashing breaks this chain.

questions.question: The word 'value' is derived from the Latin word 'valere', which means:

options.B: To be of worth / to be strong

questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: 'Valere' means to be strong or to be of worth; values are what we consider worthwhile.

questions.question: According to the NCERT document on value education, how many values were listed?
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: NCERT's 'Documents on Social, Moral and Spiritual Values in Education' listed 83 values.

questions.question: A value that is desired for its own sake, and not as a means to something else, is called a/an:
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Intrinsic (terminal) values such as truth or happiness are ends in themselves; instrumental values such as money are means to other ends.

questions.question: The five human values promoted in Sathya Sai Education in Human Values (EHV) are:
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Truth, Right Conduct, Peace, Love and Non-violence are presented as the universal human values.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of values?

options.A: Values are fixed at birth and cannot change

questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Values are acquired through socialisation and education and can change over time.

questions.question: Which set of values is enshrined in the Preamble to the Indian Constitution?
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: The Preamble secures justice, liberty and equality to all citizens and promotes fraternity.

questions.question: Which of the following is primarily a social value?
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Cooperation concerns our relations with others; the other options are mainly personal values.

questions.question: Which commission recommended a 'conscious and organised attempt' to impart education in social, moral and spiritual values?
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: The Kothari (Education) Commission stressed moral, social and spiritual values in education.

questions.question: In Krathwohl's taxonomy of the affective domain, 'Valuing' comes immediately after:
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: The order is Receiving → Responding → Valuing → Organisation → Characterisation by a value.

questions.question: Moral values are primarily concerned with:
questions.subject: Value Education – Basics
questions.explanation: Moral values such as honesty and fairness guide judgements about right and wrong behaviour.
